intro.heading_en: The Praise by Indra and the Gods (Śakrādi Stuti)
intro.carita: Madhyama Carita (the middle episode, chapters 2–4), of which this is the closing chapter. In the recitation tradition the middle carita’s presiding form is Mahālakṣmī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga (printed before chapter 2), not a statement of the Purāṇa text, which does not use the name Mahālakṣmī here. In the Gita Press pāṭha chapter 4 has no viniyoga of its own, only a dhyāna: one should meditate on Durgā called Jayā, dark as a black cloud, whose sidelong glances bring fear to the hosts of enemies, the crescent moon bound on her crown, holding in her hands conch, discus, sword and trident, three-eyed, seated on the lion’s shoulders, filling the three worlds with her radiance, surrounded by the gods and served by those who seek siddhis.
intro.summary: Medhas resumes (4.1). With Mahiṣa and his army slain, Indra and the gods, bowed and thrilling with joy, praise the Devī (4.2). Their hymn (4.3–23) bows to Ambikā, whose form is the gathered powers of all the gods but who pervades the world by her own power (4.3), whose majesty not even Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva can tell (4.4); she is fortune in the homes of the good and misfortune in the homes of the wicked, understanding, faith and modesty (4.5). The gods cannot describe her form, valour or deeds (4.6), yet name her: the cause of the worlds and the primal Prakṛti (4.7), Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8), the knowledge that liberates (4.9), the Veda whose self is sound, and Vārttā, livelihood (4.10), Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī (4.11). They recall the battle: that Mahiṣa could look on her gentle, moon-like face and still strike, and that he did not die at the sight of it in anger (4.12–13), and they pray for her grace, having seen what her anger does (4.14). Her favour brings honour, wealth and a household at peace (4.15), heaven to the doer of good (4.16), and freedom from fear to whoever remembers her (4.17). Why she kills with weapons and not with a glance: so that even her enemies, purified, reach heaven (4.18–19); their eyes were spared because they gazed at her face (4.20); compassion and relentlessness are found together in her alone (4.21–22); the worlds are saved, the enemies sent to heaven, the gods’ fear gone (4.23). In four anuṣṭubh verses they ask her protection with trident, sword, bell and bow, in every quarter, through her gentle and terrible forms and all her weapons (4.24–27). Medhas tells how the gods worshipped her with flowers of Nandana, perfumes and incense (4.28–30). The Devī offers a boon (4.31–32); the gods answer that nothing remains to be done now that Mahiṣa is dead, but ask that, whenever remembered, she destroy their calamities, and that she increase the wealth and household of any mortal who praises her with these hymns (4.33–37). Saying ‘So be it’, Bhadrakālī vanishes (4.38–39). Medhas closes the story of her rising from the gods’ bodies and announces the next: how she arose again from Gaurī’s body to slay Śumbha and Niśumbha (4.40–42).
intro.forms: Ambikā, ‘the Mother’, the name the gods use most (4.3, 4.24, 4.27, 4.37); Caṇḍikā (4.4, 4.25); Bhagavatī (4.9, 4.10, 4.34) and the sovereign titles Īśvarī (4.25) and Maheśvarī (4.35). In the hymn she is named as qualities and powers: Śrī and Alakṣmī, Buddhi, Śraddhā and Lajjā (4.5); the primal, unmanifest Prakṛti with the three guṇas (4.7); Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8); the supreme Vidyā, cause of liberation (4.9); Trayī, the Veda, whose self is sound (शब्दात्मिका), and Vārttā (4.10); Medhā, Durgā, Śrī as Viṣṇu’s consort and Gaurī as Śiva’s (4.11). The gods address her as Durgā (4.17) and as giver of boons (वरदे, 4.22), liken her angry face to Death (Antaka) enraged (4.13), and ask the protection of her gentle and her terrible forms alike (4.26). In the narrative she is ‘the sustainer of the worlds’ (जगतां धात्री, 4.29), gracious of face (प्रसादसुमुखी, 4.30), and, as she vanishes, Bhadrakālī (4.39).
intro.significance: The chapter turns the victory of chapter 3 into praise, and the praise into a promise. Its hymn is the first in the text addressed to the Goddess as warrior — Brahmā’s hymn in chapter 1 was to Yoganidrā within the sleeping Viṣṇu — and it says what the battle meant: the gods did not lend her their power (4.3), and her killing is itself compassion (4.18–23). The boon the gods ask (4.36–37) is the first statement in the text of the fruit of reciting it, which the Goddess sets out at length in chapter 12. The closing verses (4.40–42) end the middle carita and announce the third, so that the chapter is both an ending and a hinge.
intro.grammar: Most of the hymn (4.2–23) is in vasantatilakā, fourteen syllables to a printed line, so words and junctions often run across a line-end (दोषै- / र्न, 4.7; एत- / न्नीतं, 4.14; भवतीप्रसादा- / ल्लोकत्रये, 4.16); the petitions (4.24–27) return to anuṣṭubh. The hymn style is relative and correlative (या … तां त्वाम्, 4.5; यस्याः … सा, 4.4; यानि … तैः, 4.26–27), with predicates in the nominative and असि understood or stated (मेधासि, दुर्गासि, 4.11). The Goddess is the subject of second-person passives (ज्ञायसे, 4.7; उच्चार्यसे, 4.8; अभ्यस्यसे, 4.9); impersonal passives carry the wonders of the battle (प्रहृतम्, 4.12; कैर्जीव्यते, 4.13). Prayer uses the imperative (प्रसीद, पाहि, रक्ष), deliberation the first-person imperative (किं वर्णयाम, 4.6), courtesy the passive imperative (व्रियताम्, 4.32) and the respectful third person (भवती, भगवत्या). The gods’ boons are asked in epic ātmanepada optatives (हिंसेथाः, भवेथाः, 4.36–37), with the repeated participle संस्मृता संस्मृता ‘each time remembered’ (4.36).
intro.teaching: Literally, the gods praise the Goddess who has saved them, worship her, ask two boons, and she grants them and disappears; Medhas then announces the next story. As teaching, the Śākta tradition reads the hymn as a statement of who the Goddess is: one power behind fortune and misfortune, intellect and faith, sacrifice and liberation (4.5–4.11), whose anger and grace are one act — she destroys the asuras and purifies them in the same stroke (4.18–4.23). It also draws from the boon that remembrance and the recitation of these verses are enough to draw her help (4.17, 4.36–4.37). A modern reflection, which is ours and not the text’s, might add that the gods, once rescued, ask first for nothing and then for others: every mortal who will say their words. The text itself states only the hymn, the worship, the boons and her promise.
themes: The Goddess is not the sum of the gods’ powers
One Devī in fortune, intellect, faith and the Veda

conclusion.narrative: With Mahiṣa dead, the gods do what they could not do in battle: they praise. Their hymn moves from what she is — beyond the triad’s telling, Prakṛti, Svāhā and Svadhā, liberating knowledge, Veda and livelihood, Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī — to what she did, and finds in the killing a mercy that sent even her enemies to heaven. They ask her protection on every side, worship her, and, offered a boon, ask that she come whenever remembered and bless whoever recites these hymns. ‘So be it,’ says Bhadrakālī, and vanishes. Medhas closes the middle story and announces the last: her rising from Gaurī to slay Śumbha and Niśumbha (4.41–42).

constructions: The relative–correlative hymn: a या / यस्याः / यया clause taken up by तां त्वाम्, सा or ताम् (4.3–4.5), and यानि … तैः (4.26–4.27).
Second-person passives with the Goddess as subject and the agent in the instrumental (हरिहरादिभिः … न ज्ञायसे, 4.7; जनैः उच्चार्यसे, 4.8; मुनिभिः अभ्यस्यसे, 4.9).
The impersonal passive: प्रहृतं … महिषासुरेण (4.12), कैर्जीव्यते (4.13), विज्ञातम् (4.14).
Imperatives of prayer (प्रसीद, परिपालय, पाहि, रक्ष) and of deliberation (किं वर्णयाम, 4.6; केनोपमा भवतु, 4.22); the passive imperative of courtesy (व्रियताम्, 4.32).
The concessive imperative with नाम, and a thought closed by इति with मत्वा (कुर्वन्तु नाम … मत्वेति, 4.18).
The participle as a condition (स्मृता, 4.17) and its repetition for ‘every time’ (संस्मृता संस्मृता, 4.36).
Epic ātmanepada forms where classical prose has parasmaipada: हिंसेथाः, भवेथाः (4.36–37), शृणुष्व (4.42).
Agent nouns in -in and -tṛ, the latter with a genitive object (असुरक्षयकारि, 4.6; परमार्तिहन्त्री, 4.10; हन्तृ हृतदेवपराक्रमाणाम्, 4.21; धात्री, 4.29).
insights: Her form was made of the gods’ gathered powers, yet she pervades the world by her own (आत्मशक्त्या, 4.3), and even Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Śiva cannot tell her majesty (4.4, 4.7).
One Goddess is fortune and misfortune, understanding, faith and modesty (4.5), and Medhā, Durgā, Śrī and Gaurī are she alone (4.11).
The ritual word, liberating knowledge and ordinary livelihood are all her forms: Svāhā and Svadhā (4.8), the supreme vidyā (4.9), the Veda and Vārttā (4.10).
Her severity is her compassion: she slays with weapons so that the slain are purified and reach heaven (4.18–4.19, 4.23), and mercy and relentlessness are seen together in her alone (4.21–4.22).
The gentle and the terrible are one face: the moon-like face Mahiṣa struck and the angry one he survived (4.12–4.13); both kinds of form are asked to protect (4.26).
Remembrance suffices: remembered, she removes the fear of every creature (4.17), and the boon makes remembrance and recitation the way to her help (4.36–4.37).
conclusion.srividya: The hymn shares many names with the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): Ambikā (4.3; name 295, अम्बिका), Svāhā and Svadhā side by side (4.8; names 535, स्वाहा, and 536, स्वधा), Medhā, Durgā and Gaurī (4.11; names 538, मेधा, 190, दुर्गा, and 635, गौरी), Lajjā (4.5; name 740, लज्जा), the Prakṛti of the three guṇas (4.7; names 397, मूलप्रकृतिः, and 984, त्रिगुणा), Trayī (4.10; name 872, त्रयी), Caṇḍikā (4.4, 4.25; name 755, चण्डिका) and Maheśvarī (4.35; name 750, महेश्वरी). The Lalitā Sahasranāma’s अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः (name 992) is close in idea to the compassion of 4.21. These are a shared Śākta vocabulary, not evidence that one text depends on the other. The Śrī of 4.11 is Viṣṇu’s consort, not the Śrī of Śrīvidyā, and no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine — mantra, yantra or the worship of Lalitā — is stated in this chapter.

key_verses.why: The gods bow to Ambikā, whose form is the gathered powers of all the gods but who pervades the world by her own power.
She is Śrī in the homes of the virtuous and Alakṣmī in those of the wicked, understanding, faith and modesty.
Cause of the worlds, untouched by the faults of the guṇas, the whole world a portion of her: the primal, unmanifest Prakṛti.
Medhā, Durgā the boat across the ocean of existence, Śrī in Viṣṇu’s heart, Gaurī with Śiva — ‘you alone’.
Remembered, Durgā removes the fear of every creature and gives the untroubled a good mind: who but she is so tender to all?
Her nature is to end the ways of the wicked; in slaying them she has shown compassion even to her enemies.
The boon: remembered again and again, may she destroy our calamities — and the promise for whoever praises her with these hymns, completed in 4.37.

sandhi_patterns: Visarga sandhi throughout: -aḥ → -o before voiced sounds (सद्यो विनाशयसि, 4.14; पाहि नो देवि, 4.24), -ḥ → r after other vowels (दोषैर्न, 4.7; नौरसङ्गा, 4.11; कैर्जीव्यते, 4.13), -ḥ → s/ś before t/c (प्रकृतिस्त्वम्, 4.7; हरश्च, 4.4), and -āḥ losing its visarga before voiced sounds and vowels (सुरगणा निहते, 4.2; देवा ऊचुः, 4.33).

Visarga kept before a sibilant where assimilation is optional (नताः स्म, 4.3; श्रीः स्वयम्, 4.5; स्वस्थैः स्मृता, 4.17; निहतः शत्रुः, 4.35), and निश्शेष with the assimilated sibilant (4.3, the variant reads निःशेष).
Pūrvarūpa with avagraha (निहतेऽतिवीर्ये, 4.2; रिपवोऽपि, 4.19; तेऽम्बिके, 4.27), and the double avagraha for ā + ā (सदाऽऽर्द्रचित्ता, 4.17; तथाऽऽत्मनः, 4.39; मयाऽऽख्यातम्, 4.42).
Junctions across the printed line-end of the vasantatilakā stanzas (दोषै- / र्न, 4.7; तृप्तिहेतु- / रुच्चार्यसे, 4.8; एत- / न्नीतम्, 4.14; कर्मा- / ण्यत्यादृतः and भवतीप्रसादा- / ल्लोकत्रये, 4.16).

Consonant sandhi: t + ś → cch and ch doubled (उद्यच्छशाङ्कसदृशच्छवि, 4.13; तच्छृणुष्व, 4.42), t → n before n (यन्न, 4.13; यन्नागता, 4.20), t + l → ll (4.16), n + t → ṃst (अस्मांस्तथा, 4.26), and r before r dropped (तै रक्ष, 4.26).
One declared hiatus: आत्मशूलस्य | उत्तरस्याम् at the pāda break of 4.25, a metrical licence.
samasa: Long bahuvrīhis describing the gods and the Goddess (प्रणतिनम्रशिरोधरांसाः, प्रहर्षपुलकोद्गमचारुदेहाः, 4.2; निश्शेषदेवगणशक्तिसमूहमूर्त्या, 4.3; कैटभारिहृदयैककृताधिवासा, शशिमौलिकृतप्रतिष्ठा, 4.11).
Nañ compounds of the ineffable (अतुलम्, 4.4; अचिन्त्यम्, 4.6; अपारा, अव्याकृता, 4.7; अविचिन्त्यम्, अतुल्यम्, 4.21).
Upapada tatpuruṣas with agent nouns in -in (असुरक्षयकारि, 4.6; दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि, 4.17; शत्रुभयकारि, 4.22; जगत्त्रयहितैषिणी, 4.40).
Nested ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas of light (खड्गप्रभानिकरविस्फुरणैः, शूलाग्रकान्तिनिवहेन, 4.20) and of distress (परमार्तिहन्त्री, 4.10).
Bahuvrīhis in आदि (शक्रादयः, 4.2; हरिहरादिभिः, 4.7; खड्गशूलगदादीनि, 4.27; धनदारादि-, 4.37) and itaretara dvandvas (ऋग्यजुस्, 4.10; आत्मजभृत्यदाराः, 4.15; शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः, 4.41).
One avyayībhāva (प्रतिदिनम्, 4.16) and karmadhārayas of title (महेश्वरि, 4.35; भद्रकाली, 4.39).
grammar_notes: नताः स्म (4.3, 4.5) is read as ‘we are bowed’, स्म for स्मः without its visarga, as the metre requires a light syllable.
Epic ātmanepada forms are kept as ārṣa: the optatives हिंसेथाः and भवेथाः (4.36–37) and the imperative शृणुष्व (4.42).
Sentences run across verses: 4.29–4.30 (one subject, verb प्राह), 4.35–4.37 (condition, boon and the reciter’s blessing), 4.41–4.42 (the announcement of the third story).
In 4.25 the south is named with the masculine/neuter locative दक्षिणे beside the feminine locatives of the other quarters, and उत्तर is declined like a pronoun (उत्तरस्याम्).
विलोकयताम् (4.20) is a present participle in the genitive plural agreeing with असुराणाम्, not an imperative; ते in 4.23 is two words, ‘they’ and ‘to you’.
दृष्टा (4.22) agrees with the nearer of two subjects; अस्मत्तः (4.32) is the Goddess’s plural of herself.
themes: The Goddess beyond the gods’ powers
Her forms in fortune, mind and Veda
Gentle and terrible in one face
Remembrance and the fruit of recitation
uncertain: 4.3: निश्शेष (Gita Press, kept) / निःशेष (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic; the same word.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading, are flagged on 4.3 (नताः स्म as ‘we are bowed’ or the particle स्म), 4.6 (the locative सर्वेषु … असुरदेवगणादिकेषु), 4.7 (दोषैः as ‘by faults’ or as agent) and 4.37 (the construction of वित्तर्द्धिविभवैः).

comm.t: The sage Medhas resumes his story for King Suratha (and the merchant Samādhi). Chapter 3 ended with Mahiṣāsura beheaded (3.42), his army destroyed (3.43) and the gods beginning to praise the Devī (3.44); this chapter gives that praise in full. In recitation the mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa.

samasa.literal: whose bodies are beautiful with the rising of hair-thrills from great joy

morph.note: Perfect of √स्तु: reduplication तु-स्तु-, the root’s s becomes ṣ after the u of the reduplicated syllable and the t then becomes ṭ beside it (ष्टुना ष्टुः, 8.4.41); before the vowel ending -उस् the root’s u becomes uv: तुष्टुवुः ‘they praised’.
Locative absolute: participle and noun in the locative (तस्मिन् … निहते) state the circumstance ‘when he had been slain’; the agent देव्या stands in the instrumental.
Instrumental plural of वाच्: before the ending -भिः the final c becomes k and is then voiced to g (झलां जशोऽन्ते, 8.2.39).

mantras.anvaya: तस्मिन् अतिवीर्ये दुरात्मनि सुरारिबले च देव्या निहते, प्रणतिनम्रशिरोधरांसाः प्रहर्षपुलकोद्गमचारुदेहाः शक्रादयः सुरगणाः तां वाग्भिः तुष्टुवुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: A locative absolute (तस्मिन् … सुरारिबले च देव्या निहते) sets the time; the main clause is शक्रादयः सुरगणाः तां तुष्टुवुः, with two bahuvrīhi epithets of the gods and the instrument वाग्भिः.
mantras.lit: When that one of surpassing valour, the evil-souled, and the army of the gods’ enemies had been slain by the Devī, the hosts of the gods, Śakra and the rest, their necks and shoulders bent low in reverence, their bodies beautiful with hair standing on end for joy, praised her with words.
mantras.tr: When the Devī had slain that mighty, evil-hearted one and the army of the gods’ enemies, Indra and the hosts of the gods, necks and shoulders bowed in reverence, their bodies thrilling with joy, praised her in words.
mantras.tr_note: ‘That one’ (तस्मिन्) is Mahiṣāsura, who is named only in 4.12.

comm.t: The narrative frame of the hymn: Medhas tells how the gods praised the Devī after Mahiṣa’s death (3.42–44). With this stanza the text changes metre: 4.2–4.23 are in vasantatilakā, a fourteen-syllable quarter printed one quarter to a line, so a word can run over a line-end (as in 4.7–4.10); 4.24–4.27 return to anuṣṭubh.

The chapter’s colophon names it शक्रादिस्तुतिः, ‘the praise by Śakra and the others’, after the first word of this stanza. The bodily signs — bowing and the thrill of joy (pulaka) — are the classical marks of devotion: the praise is offered by the whole person, not only in words.

samasa.alt: It can also be read as a karmadhāraya qualifying आत्मशक्त्या: ‘by her own power, which is the embodied mass of the gods’ powers’. The feminine i-stem ending fits either; the bahuvrīhi, describing the Devī herself, matches chapter 2.

morph.note: Past passive participle of √तन्: the root’s nasal is lost before the participle ending (तन् + त → तत). With no copula expressed, ततम् is a finite-like predicate: ‘(this world) is pervaded’.
Imperative third singular of वि + √धा, a reduplicating (juhotyādi) root: दधा- + तु. ‘May she grant’ — the benediction that closes the first stanza.

The metre (vasantatilakā, ⏑ in the fifth syllable) needs a light syllable here, so the printed स्म cannot be a sandhi form of स्मः (which would give स्मो before v). The same phrase returns in 4.5 (नताः स्म परिपालय).

mantras.anvaya: यया निश्शेषदेवगणशक्तिसमूहमूर्त्या देव्या आत्मशक्त्या इदं जगत् ततम्, तां अखिलदेवमहर्षिपूज्याम् अम्बिकां (वयं) भक्त्या नताः स्म। सा नः शुभानि विदधातु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यया … ततम्) describes the Devī; the main clause (ताम् … नताः स्म) is the act of bowing; a separate benediction with the imperative विदधातु closes the stanza.
mantras.lit: To that Ambikā, worthy of worship by all gods and great sages — the Devī, whose form is the mass of the powers of all the hosts of gods, by whom through her own power this world is pervaded — we are bowed with devotion. May she bestow auspicious things on us.
mantras.tr: To Ambikā, worshipped by all the gods and great sages — the Devī who by her own power pervades this world, her form the gathered powers of all the hosts of gods — we bow in devotion. May she grant us what is good.
mantras.tr_note: The passive ‘by whom … is pervaded’ is turned active; ‘we bow’ renders नताः स्म.

comm.t: The first stanza of praise recalls how the Devī came to be: her body was formed from the tejas of all the gods (2.10–19). Yet the world is pervaded by her own power (आत्मशक्त्या): what the gods gave was not borrowed strength. The gods bow and ask for blessings (शुभानि).

The prayer विदधातु शुभानि सा नः has an echo in the gods’ hymn of chapter 5 (5.81: करोतु सा नः शुभहेतुरीश्वरी शुभानि). The name Ambikā, ‘Mother’, is the one the text uses most often for the warrior Goddess.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name Ambikā (name 295, अम्बिका). The two works are separate; the name is shared Śākta usage.

flags.uncertain: Variant: निश्शेष (Gita Press, kept) against निःशेष (GRETIL, Freund) — orthographic only, same word. Interpretation: नताः स्म is taken in the usual sense ‘we are bowed’ (स्म for स्मः, the visarga absent, as the metre requires); it may also be the particle स्म with the bare participle (‘bowed indeed’). The sense is the same.

morph.note: Infinitive of √वच् (वच् + तुम्, c → k before t). With अलम् it expresses capacity: न … वक्तुम् अलम् ‘not able to tell’; the verb ‘are’ is understood.
Imperative third singular of √कृ: stem करो- (tanādi u-class) + तु. मतिं करोतु ‘may she set her mind on’.
Nominative singular of भगवत् (भग + matup → -वत्): the vowel before the -nt is lengthened and the final t lost: भगवान्.

mantras.anvaya: यस्याः अतुलं प्रभावं बलं च भगवान् अनन्तः ब्रह्मा हरः च वक्तुं न हि अलम्, सा चण्डिका अखिलजगत्परिपालनाय अशुभभयस्य नाशाय च मतिं करोतु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यस्याः … अलम्, the verb ‘are’ understood) and its correlative main clause (सा चण्डिका … करोतु); two datives of purpose depend on मतिं करोतु.
mantras.lit: Whose incomparable majesty and strength the Blessed Ananta, Brahmā and Hara are indeed not able to tell — may that Caṇḍikā set her mind on the protection of the whole world and on the destruction of evil and fear.
mantras.tr: Her incomparable majesty and strength not even blessed Viṣṇu, Brahmā or Śiva can describe. May that Caṇḍikā turn her mind to protecting the whole world and to ending evil and fear.
mantras.tr_note: Ananta and Hara are named as Viṣṇu and Śiva; ‘not even’ renders the emphatic न हि.

comm.t: The three great gods of the triad cannot describe her power; the lesser gods therefore do not try to measure her but ask her to act. The prayer has two aims: protection (परिपालन) and the removal of evil and fear.

The thought that even Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva cannot describe the Goddess is a commonplace of Śākta hymns; the next stanzas (4.6–4.7) develop it. Caṇḍikā, ‘the Fierce One’, is the name from which the whole text takes its popular title, the Caṇḍī.

mantras.anvaya: या (त्वं) सुकृतिनां भवनेषु स्वयं श्रीः, पापात्मनां (भवनेषु) अलक्ष्मीः, कृतधियां हृदयेषु बुद्धिः, सतां श्रद्धा, कुलजनप्रभवस्य लज्जा (असि), तां त्वां (वयं) नताः स्म। देवि, विश्वं परिपालय।
mantras.anvaya_en: Five predicates in a relative clause (या … लज्जा, the verb ‘are’ understood), each with a genitive of the persons in whom she is that quality; the correlative ताम् त्वाम् is the object of bowing; a closing imperative.
mantras.lit: You who are yourself Śrī in the homes of the virtuous, Alakṣmī (in those) of the evil-souled, understanding in the hearts of those of cultivated mind, faith of the good, modesty of one born of a noble family — to that you we are bowed. O Devī, protect the universe.
mantras.tr: You are Fortune herself in the homes of the virtuous and Misfortune in the homes of the wicked; understanding in the hearts of the wise, faith in the good, modesty in the well-born. To you we bow: O Devī, protect the world.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Homes’ is supplied for the wicked from the first clause; ‘in the good’, ‘in the well-born’ render genitives.

comm.t: One Devī is named in five qualities, each placed in a kind of person: prosperity and its opposite, understanding, faith and modesty. The same power that blesses the virtuous is misfortune in the house of the wicked; the stanza does not make her two goddesses.

Several of these names return as forms of the Devī ‘established in all beings’ in the hymn of chapter 5: बुद्धिरूपेण (5.20-22), लज्जारूपेण (5.44-46), श्रद्धारूपेण (5.50-52), लक्ष्मीरूपेण (5.56-58). Brahmā’s hymn had already named her श्री and बुद्धि (1.79).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) includes Lajjā among the Goddess’s names (name 740, लज्जा).
A modern reading: the stanza places the divine in a household’s fortune, a mind’s clarity, a person’s faith and restraint — the Goddess is met in character as much as in temples.

mantras.anvaya: (वयं) तव एतत् अचिन्त्यं रूपं किं वर्णयाम? असुरक्षयकारि भूरि अतिवीर्यं च किम्? देवि, सर्वेषु असुरदेवगणादिकेषु आहवेषु तव अद्भुतानि चरितानि च किम् (वर्णयाम)?
mantras.anvaya_en: Three questions with one verb (वर्णयाम), each introduced by किम्: the form, the valour, the deeds. The locative सर्वेषु … असुरदेवगणादिकेषु is taken as ‘among all the hosts’ (the battles fought among them).
mantras.lit: How should we describe this unthinkable form of yours? And (how) the abundant, surpassing valour that destroys the asuras? And (how), O Devī, your wondrous deeds in battles, among all the hosts of asuras, gods and the rest?
mantras.tr: How can we describe this form of yours, beyond all thought? Or your boundless valour that destroys the asuras? Or the wonders you have done in battle, O Devī, among all the hosts of gods, asuras and others?

comm.t: The gods confess that their praise cannot match its object: three questions, each beginning with किम्, about her form, her valour and her deeds. The hymn returns to the same three — form (रूप), valour (वीर्य) and conduct — in 4.21.
The confession of inadequacy is a convention of Sanskrit hymns, but here it follows directly on 4.4: if Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva cannot describe her power, the lesser gods can only wonder at it.
A modern reading: worship begins where description fails. The questions are not a refusal to speak but a way of speaking that keeps the mystery open.

flags.uncertain: The locative सर्वेषु … असुरदेवगणादिकेषु can be read ‘(in battles) among all the hosts of asuras, gods and others’ or, as a locative of reference, ‘(wondrous) to all the hosts …’. The first is followed here.

morph.note: Passive present of √ज्ञा: stem ज्ञाय- (ज्ञा + yak) with the ātmanepada ending -से, second singular: ‘you are known’. The agent of a passive is put in the instrumental, so दोषैः can be read as agent (see flags).
Past participle of वि + आ + √कृ (व्याकृत ‘separated out, made distinct’) with the negative अ-: the Sāṃkhya-Vedānta term for the undifferentiated cause before creation.
आद्य is आदि ‘beginning’ + the taddhita -य (the final i dropped): ‘being at the beginning, primal’; feminine आद्या.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) समस्तजगतां हेतुः (असि)। त्रिगुणा अपि दोषैः न ज्ञायसे। हरिहरादिभिः अपि अपारा (असि)। सर्वाश्रया (असि); इदम् अखिलं जगत् (तव) अंशभूतम्; त्वं हि आद्या परमा अव्याकृता प्रकृतिः (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A string of predicates of an unexpressed त्वम्, one finite verb (ज्ञायसे, passive), a nominal clause about the world (जगत् अंशभूतम्), and the reason, introduced by हि: you are the primal Prakṛti.
mantras.lit: (You are) the cause of all the worlds; though possessed of the three guṇas, you are not known by faults; (you are) unfathomable even by Hari, Hara and the others; the support of all — this whole world is (your) portion; for you are the unmanifest, supreme, primal Prakṛti.
mantras.tr: You are the cause of all the worlds. Though you bear the three guṇas, no fault of theirs is found in you; even Viṣṇu, Śiva and the other gods cannot reach your farther shore. You are the support of all, and this whole world is but a portion of you, for you are the primal Prakṛti, supreme and unmanifest.
mantras.tr_note: ‘No fault of theirs is found in you’ follows the usual reading of दोषैः न ज्ञायसे (‘you are not known (to be touched) by faults’); see flags for the other.

comm.t: The hymn turns from her deeds to her nature: she is the cause of the worlds and the primal, unmanifest Prakṛti, of which the world is only a part. The paradox of the first line: she has the three guṇas, yet their faults do not cling to her. Even Hari and Hara do not reach her farther shore.

The vocabulary is Sāṃkhya (prakṛti, the three guṇas, avyākṛta), but the Prakṛti of this hymn is not an unconscious matter set against spirit: she is the Goddess herself, the cause and support of all. Brahmā’s hymn says the same (1.78: प्रकृतिस्त्वं च सर्वस्य गुणत्रयविभाविनी).
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess मूलप्रकृतिः (name 397) and त्रिगुणा (name 984) — the same two ideas in a different text.

flags.uncertain: दोषैः न ज्ञायसे admits two readings: ‘you are not known (to be touched) by faults’ (the usual one, followed in tr) or, with दोषैः as the agent of the passive, ‘you are not known by (those who have) faults’. Both are grammatical.

स्वाहा and स्वधा are indeclinable ritual words, the calls that accompany offerings to the gods and to the ancestors. The hymn treats them as names of the Goddess and makes them predicates (‘you are Svāhā’).

mantras.anvaya: देवि, सकलेषु मखेषु यस्याः समुदीरणेन समस्तसुरता तृप्तिं प्रयाति, (सा त्वं) स्वाहा असि वै। पितृगणस्य च तृप्तिहेतुः (त्वम्), अतः एव त्वं जनैः स्वधा च उच्चार्यसे।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यस्याः … प्रयाति) and its main clause (स्वाहा असि वै), then a second sentence with a passive verb whose agent is जनैः and whose predicate nominative is स्वधा.
mantras.lit: O Devī, you by whose utterance in all sacrifices the whole company of the gods attains satisfaction — you are indeed Svāhā; and, being the cause of the satisfaction of the host of ancestors, for that very reason you are pronounced by people as Svadhā too.
mantras.tr: O Devī, at every sacrifice it is by the uttering of you that all the gods together are satisfied: you are Svāhā. And because you satisfy the host of the ancestors, people utter you as Svadhā.

comm.t: Svāhā is spoken as an oblation is poured into the fire for the gods; Svadhā when it is offered to the ancestors. The hymn identifies the Goddess with these sacred words themselves: the gods and the ancestors are fed through her.

Brahmā’s hymn in chapter 1 already said त्वं स्वाहा त्वं स्वधा (1.73). Here the identification is explained: she is Svāhā because the gods are satisfied by her utterance, Svadhā because the ancestors are.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the same pair of names side by side: स्वाहा (name 535) and स्वधा (name 536).

samasa.alt: The feminine ending (व्रत is neuter) shows a bahuvrīhi. Whether the ‘great vow’ is the Goddess’s own or the discipline by which the sages reach her is left open by the compound; the next words (अभ्यस्यसे … मुनिभिः) favour the second.

morph.note: Passive present of अभि + √अस् ‘to throw’ (divādi अस्यति): with अभि it means ‘to practise, repeat, apply oneself to’. The agent is मुनिभिः: the Goddess is the object of the sages’ discipline.
Instrumental plural of the in-stem अर्थिन् ‘one who seeks’ (from अर्थ ‘aim’): -इभिः.
With the correlative सा and the adjectives परमा, भगवती, the predicate picks up 1.57 (सा विद्या परमा मुक्तेर्हेतुभूता सनातनी).

mantras.anvaya: देवि, या त्वं मुक्तिहेतुः अविचिन्त्यमहाव्रता (असि), सुनियतेन्द्रियतत्त्वसारैः अस्तसमस्तदोषैः मोक्षार्थिभिः मुनिभिः अभ्यस्यसे, सा (त्वं) परमा भगवती विद्या असि हि।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … अभ्यस्यसे) with two predicates and a passive verb whose agent is मुनिभिः and its three epithets; the main clause is सा … विद्या असि.
mantras.lit: You who are the cause of liberation, whose great vow is unthinkable, who are practised by sages seeking liberation, their senses well restrained, holding reality as the essence, all faults cast off — you are that supreme, blessed Knowledge, O Devī.
mantras.tr: You are the cause of liberation, your great discipline beyond thought. Sages who seek release — senses held in check, intent on the truth, every fault cast off — make you their practice. You, O Devī, are that blessed and supreme Knowledge.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Make you their practice’ turns the passive अभ्यस्यसे (‘you are practised’) active.

comm.t: After the ritual words of 4.8 the hymn names the Goddess as the goal of contemplative practice: the knowledge (vidyā) that liberates, pursued by disciplined sages.

The stanza echoes Medhas’s teaching in chapter 1: सा विद्या परमा मुक्तेर्हेतुभूता सनातनी (1.57), and the gods’ hymn in chapter 11 calls her मुक्तिहेतुः again (11.5). The same Goddess who binds as Mahāmāyā (1.55) is the knowledge that releases.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also names the Goddess विद्या (name 549) and मुक्तिरूपिणी (name 737).

mantras.anvaya: (त्वं) शब्दात्मिका सुविमलर्ग्यजुषाम् उद्गीथरम्यपदपाठवतां साम्नां च निधानम् (असि)। भगवती देवी (त्वं) भवभावनाय त्रयी (असि), सर्वजगतां परमार्तिहन्त्री वार्ता च (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Nominal sentences with the verb ‘are’ understood. भवभावनाय is taken with त्रयी (the Veda for the world’s sustenance); it may also go with both त्रयी and वार्ता.
mantras.lit: Having sound as your self, you are the repository of the very pure Ṛk and Yajus and of the Sāmans, which possess a recitation of words delightful with the udgītha. You, the Blessed Devī, are the Triple (Veda) for the bringing-forth of the world, and Vārttā, the destroyer of the supreme distress of all the worlds.
mantras.tr: Your very self is sound: you are the treasure-house of the spotless Ṛk and Yajus and of the Sāman chants, lovely in their words with the udgītha. Blessed Devī, you are the Triple Veda, for the sustaining of the world, and you are Vārttā, the livelihood that ends the deepest distress of all the worlds.
mantras.tr_note: Vārttā, a technical name, is glossed as ‘livelihood’ (agriculture, cattle and trade); ‘sustaining’ interprets भावन ‘causing to be’.

comm.t: The Goddess is the Veda as sound: the Ṛk, the Yajus and the sung Sāman, whose central chant is the udgītha. She is also Vārttā, the knowledge by which people earn their living: the sacred and the practical are both her forms.

Trayī (the threefold Veda) and Vārttā (agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade) are two of the four branches of knowledge in the classical list known from the Arthaśāstra, with ānvīkṣikī (reasoning) and daṇḍanīti (government). Brahmā’s hymn had called her स्वरात्मिका, ‘whose self is the sounded syllable’ (1.73); here she is शब्दात्मिका.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess त्रयी (name 872).

A play on words: दुर्गा ‘the hard-to-reach’ is the boat across the दुर्ग, the hard-to-cross, ocean of existence. दुर्ग is दुर् + √गम् (‘hard to go’).

mantras.anvaya: देवि, (त्वं) विदिताखिलशास्त्रसारा मेधा असि; असङ्गा दुर्गभवसागरनौः दुर्गा असि; कैटभारिहृदयैककृताधिवासा श्रीः (असि); शशिमौलिकृतप्रतिष्ठा गौरी (च) त्वम् एव (असि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Four identifications, each name with its epithet: Medhā, Durgā, Śrī, Gaurī. त्वम् एव in the last line sums them up: you alone are all of them.
mantras.lit: You are Medhā, O Devī, by whom the essence of all the śāstras is known; you are Durgā, the boat across the hard-to-cross ocean of existence, unattached; Śrī, who has made her dwelling in the heart of Kaiṭabha’s foe alone; you alone are Gaurī, who has made her place in the moon-crested one.
mantras.tr: O Devī, you are Medhā, who knows the essence of every scripture; you are Durgā, the boat across the perilous ocean of worldly life, yourself untouched by attachment. You are Śrī, whose one dwelling is the heart of Viṣṇu, Kaiṭabha’s foe; and you alone are Gaurī, established with the moon-crowned Śiva.
mantras.tr_note: Kaiṭabha’s foe and the moon-crested one are named as Viṣṇu and Śiva.

comm.t: Four goddesses are named — Medhā (learning), Durgā, Śrī (Lakṣmī, consort of Viṣṇu, who killed Kaiṭabha in chapter 1) and Gaurī (consort of Śiva) — and the last line says that the Devī alone is all of them. The word-play दुर्गा / दुर्ग makes Durgā the boat across the ocean that is hard to cross.

The Devī herself later gives another account of the name Durgā: she will slay the asura Durgama and be known as Durgā (11.50). The stanza is often read as a statement of the Śākta teaching that the consorts of the gods are forms of the one Goddess.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has three of these names: मेधा (name 538), दुर्गा (name 190) and गौरी (name 635).

mantras.anvaya: (देवि,) ईषत्सहासम् अमलं परिपूर्णचन्द्रबिम्बानुकारि कनकोत्तमकान्तिकान्तं (तव) वक्त्रं विलोक्य तथा अपि आत्तरुषा महिषासुरेण सहसा प्रहृतम् (इति यत्, तत्) अत्यद्भुतम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The statement ‘Mahiṣāsura, having seen your face, struck’ (an impersonal passive with the agent in the instrumental) is the subject of the predicate अत्यद्भुतम्. The stanza is answered by 4.13 (‘but that, seeing it angry, he did not die at once — that is more wonderful’).
mantras.lit: Having looked at (your) face — gently smiling, spotless, resembling the orb of the full moon, lovely with the lustre of the finest gold — that even so a blow was suddenly struck by Mahiṣāsura, seized with wrath, (is) exceedingly wonderful.
mantras.tr: Your face was gently smiling and spotless, like the orb of the full moon, lovely with the glow of finest gold; that Mahiṣāsura could look on it and even so, seized by fury, strike out at once — that is a great wonder.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Your’ is supplied (the face is the Devī’s); the impersonal passive is turned active.

comm.t: The hymn turns to the battle of chapter 3 and to the Devī’s face. Its beauty — smiling, pure, moon-like, golden — should have disarmed the asura; that he could see it and still strike is the first wonder. The second, greater wonder follows in 4.13: that seeing the same face in anger he did not die on the spot.

The pair 4.12–4.13 sets the Devī’s gentle (saumya) and terrible (raudra) aspects side by side: the same face is lovely and dreadful. The gods’ astonishment is also a judgement on Mahiṣa’s blindness: the asura sees beauty and answers it with violence.
A modern reading: the stanza asks what it takes to look at goodness and still choose to attack it. Anger (रुष्) is named as what blinds.

Impersonal passive (bhāve prayoga) of the intransitive √जीव्: there is no grammatical subject, and the one who lives is put in the instrumental (कैः). The question is rhetorical: no one lives.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, कुपितं भ्रुकुटीकरालम् उद्यच्छशाङ्कसदृशच्छवि (तव वक्त्रं) दृष्ट्वा तु महिषः यत् सद्यः प्राणान् न मुमोच, तत् अतीव चित्रम्। हि कुपितान्तकदर्शनेन कैः जीव्यते?
mantras.anvaya_en: The face of 4.12 (वक्त्रम्) is the understood object of दृष्ट्वा. The यत्-clause is the subject that तत् resumes: ‘that he did not die — that is most strange’. The last line is a rhetorical question in the impersonal passive.
mantras.lit: But having seen (your face), O Devī, angry, dreadful with its frown, its hue like the rising moon — that Mahiṣa did not at once give up his life, that is exceedingly strange; for by whom is it lived after the sight of Death enraged?
mantras.tr: But, O Devī, Mahiṣa saw your face in anger — dreadful with its frown, flushed like the rising moon — and did not die on the spot: that is the stranger wonder. For who can live once he has looked on Death enraged?
mantras.tr_note: ‘Your face’ is supplied from वक्त्रम् in 4.12. ‘The stranger wonder’ renders अतीव चित्रम् ‘exceedingly strange’, which answers the अत्यद्भुतम् of 4.12.

comm.t: The gods continue the paradox of 4.12. That Mahiṣa could strike the gentle, smiling face was strange; that he survived the sight of the same face in anger is stranger still, for the angry Goddess is Death (Antaka) himself.

The two verses are read as a pair: the Goddess is seen first as gentle and then as terrible, the two kinds of form that 4.26 names together (सौम्यानि … अत्यर्थघोराणि). The rising moon is red, so the comparison gives the colour of anger while keeping the moon of 4.12.

samasa.alt: Also analysed with the middle member dropped: महिषरूपः असुरः, ‘the asura in buffalo form’. Since महिष is his name in 4.13 and throughout, the plain appositional reading fits.

morph.note: √सद् takes the stem सीद- in the present system: प्र-सीद ‘settle down, become clear’, and so ‘be pleased, be gracious’.
Causative of √नश् ‘perish’: the root vowel is lengthened (नाश्) and -अय- added — ‘cause to perish’, destroy.
With अस्तम् this is an idiom: अस्तं नी ‘lead to the setting (as of the sun)’, i.e. bring to an end. The agent, ‘by you’, is understood.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, प्रसीद। परमा भवती भवाय (भवति); कोपवती (सती त्वं) सद्यः कुलानि विनाशयसि। यत् एतत् सुविपुलं महिषासुरस्य बलम् अस्तं नीतम्, एतत् अधुना एव विज्ञातम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Line 1 is a prayer followed by a nominal clause (‘you are for welfare’); line 2 states the opposite (‘angry, you destroy’). In lines 3–4 the first एतत् ‘this’ is explained by the यत्-clause.
mantras.lit: O Devī, be gracious. You, supreme, are for (our) welfare; angry, you at once destroy whole families. This has been known just now, that this very vast army of Mahiṣāsura has been brought to its end.
mantras.tr: Be gracious, O Devī! Supreme, you are there for our flourishing; in anger you destroy whole races in a moment. We have seen it just now: the vast army of Mahiṣāsura has been brought to nothing.
mantras.tr_note: The contrast of line 1 with कोपवती ‘when angry’ is left implicit, as in the Sanskrit. ‘We have seen it’ renders the impersonal विज्ञातम् ‘it has been known’.

comm.t: A plea, and the lesson of the battle just ended. The same Goddess who is supreme for the world’s welfare destroys whole races when angered; the gods have just watched Mahiṣa’s army go down.

The sound-play भवती / भवाय (‘you’ / ‘for welfare’) is in the Sanskrit. The verse is read as the reason for the prayer प्रसीद: the face of anger has done its work, and the gods ask her to turn to them the face of grace.

morph.note: Past participle of सम् + √मन्: the root’s nasal drops before -त (मन् + त → मत). ‘Thought well of’, honoured.
Present of √सद् ‘sit, sink’ (stem सीद-). The same root with प्र gives प्रसन्ना in line 4: their dharma does not sink, because she is ‘settled’ in grace towards them.
Past participle of प्र + √सद्: the d of the root and the t of the suffix both become n (सद् + त → सन्न). With the genitive येषाम्: ‘gracious to whom’.

mantras.anvaya: येषां (प्रति) अभ्युदयदा भवती सदा प्रसन्ना (भवति), ते जनपदेषु सम्मताः, तेषां धनानि, तेषां यशांसि, (तेषां) धर्मवर्गः च न सीदति; निभृतात्मजभृत्यदाराः ते एव धन्याः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The relative clause of line 4 (येषां … प्रसन्ना) defines the ते of lines 1 and 3. The main clauses are nominal (‘theirs are riches’) except सीदति.
mantras.lit: They are honoured in the lands; theirs are riches, theirs are glories, and their body of dharma does not sink; blessed indeed are they, whose sons, servants and wives are loyal — to whom you, giver of prosperity, are always gracious.
mantras.tr: Those to whom you, the giver of prosperity, are always gracious are honoured in every land. Wealth is theirs, and fame, and their righteousness never fails. Blessed are they, and loyal their sons, their servants and their wives.
mantras.tr_note: The relative clause of line 4 is placed first in English.

comm.t: The fruits of her grace in this world are listed: honour, wealth, fame, a dharma that does not fail and a household at peace. All of them hang on the condition of the last line: that she is gracious (प्रसन्ना).

The verse turns from the battle to the worshipper. Its blessings are the householder’s abhyudaya, worldly flourishing; the next verse carries them on to heaven, and the hymn’s closing requests (4.37) ask for the same wealth, family and prosperity for whoever recites it.

she who gives deeds their reward

A particle that asserts while inviting assent: ‘surely you are …, are you not?’

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, सुकृती अत्यादृतः (सन्) प्रतिदिनं सकलानि धर्म्याणि कर्माणि सदा एव करोति, ततः च भवतीप्रसादात् स्वर्गं प्रयाति। तेन (हे) देवि, (त्वं) लोकत्रये अपि फलदा ननु।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses with one subject (सुकृती): he does the deeds, and then reaches heaven through her grace. The conclusion (तेन … ननु) is a nominal sentence with ‘you’ understood.
mantras.lit: O Devī, the man of merit, with great care, every day always performs all righteous deeds; and then, through your grace, he goes to heaven. Therefore, O Devī, are you not the giver of fruit even in the three worlds?
mantras.tr: O Devī, the virtuous man performs every righteous deed, day after day, with devoted care, and then by your grace he goes to heaven. So is it not you, O Devī, who give the fruit of action in all three worlds?
mantras.tr_note: ननु is rendered as a question expecting ‘yes’.

comm.t: The good man’s deeds bear their fruit only through her grace (भवतीप्रसादात्). The gods conclude that she is the giver of reward in all three worlds, not in heaven alone.
Ritual duty is not set aside: it is done daily and with care. But its fruit comes from her favour, and this is why, in the Śākta tradition, devotion is joined to duty rather than replacing it.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess स्वर्गापवर्गदा (name 764), ‘giver of heaven and of release’. The Devī Māhātmya speaks here of heaven and of fruit in the three worlds; release is the subject of 4.9 (मुक्तिहेतुः).

morph.note: A passive participle with the force of a condition: ‘(when you are) remembered’. In line 2 its agent is स्वस्थैः; in line 1 the agent is left open, so anyone at all who remembers her.

Vocative of the feminine of हारिन् (√हृ + -इन्, ‘taking away’), which adds -ई: हारिणी, voc. हारिणि.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) दुर्गे, स्मृता (त्वम्) अशेषजन्तोः भीतिं हरसि; स्वस्थैः स्मृता (त्वम्) अतीव शुभां मतिं ददासि। (हे) दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि, सर्वोपकारकरणाय सदा आर्द्रचित्ता त्वदन्या का (अस्ति)?
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel clauses, each conditioned by स्मृता; then a rhetorical question, ‘who other than you …?’, whose answer is ‘no one’.
mantras.lit: O Durgā, remembered, you take away the fear of every creature; remembered by those at ease, you give an exceedingly auspicious understanding. O remover of poverty, sorrow and fear, who other than you is always tender-hearted for doing good to all?
mantras.tr: O Durgā, when you are remembered you take away the fear of every creature; remembered by those at ease, you give a mind turned wholly to the good. Remover of poverty, sorrow and fear — who but you has a heart ever tender, ready to help all?

comm.t: Two kinds of people remember her: any creature in fear, whose fear she removes, and those at ease (स्वस्थैः), to whom she gives a good understanding. The verse ends by asking who else is so tender towards all; the unspoken answer is no one.

Remembrance alone (स्मृता) is enough; no rite or offering is named. The verse is one of the seven gathered in the Saptaślokī Durgā, a short devotional selection from the Saptaśatī, and it is among the best known of the whole text.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the names दुर्गा (190), दुःखहन्त्री (191) and भयापहा (121), close to this verse’s दुर्गे and दारिद्र्यदुःखभयहारिणि. The parallel is one of epithets; the two hymns are separate works.

samasa.sense: a warrior’s death on the field

morph.note: Imperative with the particle नाम has concessive force: ‘let them indeed do (sin)’, i.e. ‘granted that they sin’. It sets up the contrast with प्रयान्तु ‘(yet) let them go (to heaven)’.

mantras.anvaya: एभिः हतैः जगत् सुखम् उपैति; तथा एते चिराय नरकाय पापं कुर्वन्तु नाम, (तथापि) संग्राममृत्युम् अधिगम्य दिवं प्रयान्तु — इति मत्वा नूनं (हे) देवि, (त्वम्) अहितान् विनिहंसि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Lines 1–3 are the Goddess’s thought as the gods imagine it, closed by इति; the main clause is मत्वा … विनिहंसि.
mantras.lit: ‘By these being slain the world attains happiness; and likewise these — granted they do sin (leading) to hell for long — having met death in battle, let them go to heaven’: having thought thus, surely, you strike down the enemies, O Devī.
mantras.tr: ‘With these slain, the world will find happiness; and though they have earned a long hell by their sins, let them meet death in battle and go to heaven’ — surely it is with this thought, O Devī, that you strike your enemies down.
mantras.tr_note: कुर्वन्तु नाम (‘let them do, granted’) is rendered as a concession, ‘though they have earned … by their sins’.

comm.t: The gods explain why she kills: the world is freed, and the slain asuras themselves, whatever their sins, reach heaven through death in battle at her hands. One act serves both the world and the killed.

That death in battle opens heaven belongs to the warrior ethic of the epics and Purāṇas; the hymn applies it to the Goddess’s enemies. With 4.19–20 it builds the theme the gods state outright in 4.21: her compassion reaches even her enemies (वैरिष्वपि … दया).
A modern reading: the verse refuses to divide beings into those who deserve good and those who do not. Even her destruction is imagined as a form of care.

mantras.anvaya: (हे देवि) भवती दृष्ट्वा एव सर्वासुरान् भस्म किं न प्रकरोति, यत् अरिषु शस्त्रं प्रहिणोषि? ‘रिपवः अपि शस्त्रपूताः (सन्तः) लोकान् प्रयान्तु’ हि — इत्थं तेषु अपि ते मतिः अतिसाध्वी भवति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A question (किं न … प्रकरोति), whose occasion is the यत्-clause (‘that you hurl a weapon’). Line 3 gives the Goddess’s own wish as the answer; line 4 is the gods’ verdict on it.
mantras.lit: Why do you not make all the asuras ash merely by looking, that you hurl a weapon at the enemies? ‘Let even the enemies, purified by the weapon, go to the worlds’ — for thus is your thought, exceedingly kind even towards them.
mantras.tr: Why do you not burn all the asuras to ash with a single glance, but hurl your weapons at them instead? Because you would have even your enemies, made pure by your weapons, reach the higher worlds. So kind is your intent, even towards them.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Because’ renders हि; ‘the higher worlds’ interprets लोकान् ‘the worlds’, as 4.18 (दिवं प्रयान्तु) shows.

comm.t: The gods answer their own question. She could destroy the asuras by sight alone, but she uses weapons so that their touch may purify her enemies and send them to the higher worlds. Even her choice of weapon is an act of kindness.

The verse carries 4.18 further: death at the Goddess’s hand is read as purification (पूत), not only punishment. The tradition draws from it that her anger and her grace are one act seen from two sides.

mantras.anvaya: खड्गप्रभानिकरविस्फुरणैः उग्रैः तथा शूलाग्रकान्तिनिवहेन तव अंशुमदिन्दुखण्डयोग्याननं विलोकयताम् असुराणां दृशः यत् विलयं न आगताः, तत् एतत् (तव आननस्य दर्शनस्य फलम्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The यत्-clause carries the fact: the asuras’ eyes were not destroyed. तत् एतत् ‘that is this’ points to the participle phrase as its reason: they were gazing at your face.
mantras.lit: That, by the fierce flashings of the mass of the sword’s light and likewise by the stream of lustre from the trident’s point, the eyes of the asuras did not go to destruction, (they) gazing at your face fit for the radiant crescent of the moon — that is this.
mantras.tr: The blazing flashes of your sword and the flood of light from the point of your trident did not destroy the asuras’ eyes — because they were gazing at your face, like the radiant crescent of the moon.
mantras.tr_note: तत् एतत् (‘that is this’) points to the participle विलोकयताम् as the reason; English makes it ‘because’.

comm.t: Another wonder of the battle: the glare of her weapons should have blinded the asuras, but their eyes were not destroyed. The gods give the reason: they were looking at her face, which is like the moon.

The moon is the standing image of what cools and soothes; the verse sets it against the fierce light of sword and trident. The same face that terrifies in 4.13 here protects even her enemies, the theme of 4.18–21.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also likens her face to the moon: शरच्चन्द्रनिभानना (name 129), ‘whose face is like the autumn moon’. The image is shared devotional language; the works are separate.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, तव शीलं दुर्वृत्तवृत्तशमनम्; तथा एतत् रूपम् अविचिन्त्यम् अन्यैः अतुल्यं (च); वीर्यं च हृतदेवपराक्रमाणां हन्तृ; इत्थं त्वया वैरिषु अपि दया प्रकटिता एव।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three nominal sentences (on शील, रूप and वीर्य), then a passive verdict (दया … प्रकटिता) with त्वया as agent; इत्थम् sums up what 4.18–20 described.
mantras.lit: O Devī, your nature is the quelling of the conduct of the wicked; likewise this form is inconceivable and unequalled by others; and (your) valour is the slayer of those who had robbed the gods of their prowess; thus compassion has indeed been shown by you even towards enemies.
mantras.tr: O Devī, it is your nature to put an end to the ways of the wicked; your form is beyond thought, and none can equal it; your valour destroys those who robbed the gods of their might — and in this way you have shown compassion even to your enemies.

comm.t: The gods sum up the Goddess under three heads, her nature (शील), her form (रूप) and her valour (वीर्य), and draw the conclusion of 4.18–20: in this very way, by slaying them in battle, she has shown compassion even to her enemies.

The three heads echo the gods’ earlier question in 4.6 (रूपमचिन्त्यमेतत्, अतिवीर्यम्, चरितानि). The point traditionally drawn is that her severity is itself mercy: the act that protects the gods also purifies the asuras.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) calls the Goddess अव्याजकरुणामूर्तिः (name 992), ‘compassion embodied, without a pretext’. The Devī Māhātmya makes a related point by example: compassion shown to those who did nothing to earn it.

mantras.lit: With what can there be a comparison of this valour of yours? And where (is) a form fear-causing to enemies (and) exceedingly captivating? Compassion in the heart and relentlessness in battle are seen, O Devī, giver of boons, in you alone, even in the three worlds.
mantras.tr: To what could this valour of yours be compared? Where else is a form that strikes terror into enemies and yet captivates the heart? Compassion within and relentlessness in battle — in all three worlds, O Devī, giver of boons, these are seen together in you alone.
mantras.tr_note: ‘The heart’ after ‘captivates’ is supplied: अतिहारि means ‘exceedingly taking (the mind)’. ‘Together’ makes explicit what एव implies: the pair is found nowhere else.

comm.t: Nothing compares with her valour; no other form is at once terrible to enemies and supremely beautiful; nowhere in the three worlds are tenderness of heart and hardness in battle found together, except in her.

The verse names the paradox the hymn has been describing since 4.13: the gentle and the terrible, mercy and severity, held in one person. In the Śākta tradition this union of opposites is a mark of the supreme Goddess.

mantras.anvaya: त्वया रिपुनाशनेन एतत् अखिलं त्रैलोक्यं त्रातम्; समरमूर्धनि हत्वा ते रिपुगणाः अपि (त्वया) दिवं नीताः; अस्माकम् उन्मदसुरारिभवं भयम् अपि अपास्तम्। ते नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three passive clauses with the one agent त्वया (त्रातम्, नीताः, अपास्तम्), then the salutation नमस्ते.
mantras.lit: This entire triple world has been saved by you through the destruction of the enemies; having slain (them) at the head of battle, they too, the hosts of enemies, have been led to heaven; and our fear, arising from the frenzied enemies of the gods, has been cast away. Salutation to you!
mantras.tr: By destroying the enemies you have saved these three worlds entire. Slaying them at the forefront of battle, you have led even those enemy hosts to heaven; and you have driven away our fear of the frenzied foes of the gods. Salutation to you!
mantras.tr_note: The passives (त्रातम्, नीताः, अपास्तम्) are turned into active sentences with ‘you’ as subject.

comm.t: The hymn sums up what the Goddess has done: the three worlds saved, the enemies themselves sent to heaven, and the gods’ fear removed. It closes the long vasantatilakā praise with नमस्ते.

Three beneficiaries are named in order, the world, the slain enemies and the gods, so the verse gathers the themes of 4.18–22. After the salutation the gods turn from praise to petition: the anuṣṭubh verses that follow (4.24–27) ask for protection.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) देवि, शूलेन नः पाहि; (हे) अम्बिके, खड्गेन च (नः) पाहि; घण्टास्वनेन चापज्यानिःस्वनेन च नः पाहि।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three imperatives (पाहि) with one object (नः) and four instruments: trident, sword, the bell’s sound, the bowstring’s twang.
mantras.lit: With the trident protect us, O Devī; protect (us) with the sword too, O Ambikā; with the sound of the bell protect us, and with the twang of the bowstring.
mantras.tr: Protect us with your trident, O Devī; protect us with your sword, O Mother; protect us with the ringing of your bell and the twang of your bowstring.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Your’ is supplied throughout: these are the weapons the gods gave her in 2.20–24.

comm.t: The hymn changes metre and mood: from the long vasantatilakā praises the gods turn to a short anuṣṭubh prayer for protection. Four of her attributes are invoked: trident, sword, bell and bow, each a god’s gift in 2.20–24 (Śiva’s trident, Vāyu’s bow, Indra’s bell from Airāvata, Kāla’s sword).

Even the sounds of her weapons protect: the bell, whose ringing stunned the asuras (घण्टास्वनविमोहितान्, 2.56), and the bowstring, whose twang shook the worlds (धनुर्ज्यानिःस्वनेन, 2.38). The four verses 4.24–27 are often recited on their own as a prayer for protection.

A metrical licence, printed so in the Gita Press text.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) चण्डिके, प्राच्यां (नः) रक्ष, प्रतीच्यां च (रक्ष), दक्षिणे रक्ष; तथा (हे) ईश्वरि, आत्मशूलस्य भ्रामणेन उत्तरस्यां (रक्ष)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A series of imperatives with ‘us’ understood from 4.24. The instrumental भ्रामणेनात्मशूलस्य can go with the north alone or, through तथा ‘likewise’, with all four quarters.
mantras.lit: In the east protect (us), and in the west; O Caṇḍikā, protect (us) in the south; by the whirling of your own trident, likewise in the north, O Īśvarī.
mantras.tr: Protect us in the east and in the west, O Caṇḍikā; protect us in the south; and in the north as well, O Sovereign Lady, by the whirling of your trident.

comm.t: The prayer now covers space: the four quarters are named one by one, and her own trident, whirled about her, is the guard.

Guarding the quarters is the usual plan of protective prayers (kavacas), in which each direction is given a guardian; the Devī Kavaca recited before the Saptaśatī in the Gita Press pāṭha follows that plan. Here one Goddess guards them all.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name चण्डिका (755), the name by which the Devī Māhātmya addresses her here and throughout. The shared name belongs to a shared Śākta vocabulary; the works are separate.

The correlative of both relative clauses (यानि … यानि च …): ‘with those (forms)’.
Accusative singular of the feminine root-noun भू ‘earth’.

mantras.anvaya: यानि ते सौम्यानि रूपाणि त्रैलोक्ये विचरन्ति, यानि च अत्यर्थघोराणि (रूपाणि त्रैलोक्ये विचरन्ति), तैः अस्मान् तथा भुवं रक्ष।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two relative clauses (यानि … यानि च …) taken up by one correlative (तैः), then the imperative with two objects.
mantras.lit: Your gentle forms which move about in the three worlds, and those which are terrible beyond measure — with them protect us and the earth as well.
mantras.tr: With all your forms that roam the three worlds, the gentle ones and those terrible beyond measure, protect us, and the earth as well.

comm.t: After the quarters of space, the forms of the Goddess: her gentle forms and her terrible ones alike are asked to guard the gods and the earth.

The pairing of gentle (सौम्य) and terrible (घोर) forms is basic to Śākta thought; both are hers, and both protect. The hymn has shown both: the moon-like face of 4.12 and 4.20 and the face of wrath in 4.13.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) includes the name सौम्या (910), ‘the gentle one’. The Devī Māhātmya asks for the protection of the gentle and the terrible forms together.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अम्बिके, खड्गशूलगदादीनि करपल्लवसङ्गीनि यानि च ते अस्त्राणि (सन्ति), तैः अस्मान् सर्वतः रक्ष।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (यानि … अस्त्राणि) taken up by the correlative तैः; the imperative रक्ष ends the hymn’s petitions.
mantras.lit: And your weapons, O Ambikā — sword, trident, mace and the rest — which cling to your sprout-like hands: with them protect us on every side.
mantras.tr: And with all your weapons, O Mother — sword, trident, mace and the rest — that rest in your tender hands, protect us on every side.

comm.t: The last petition of the hymn: all her weapons, held in her soft hands, are asked to guard the gods from every side. It completes the prayer begun in 4.24 with trident and sword.

Terrible weapons in leaf-tender hands repeat in small the hymn’s theme of the gentle and the fierce in one Goddess. With this verse the Śakrādi Stuti ends; the narrative resumes at 4.28, and the gods worship her with flowers and incense (4.29–30).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name शूलाद्यायुधसम्पन्ना (506), ‘endowed with the trident and other weapons’, built with the same ‘X and the rest’ (आदि) pattern as खड्गशूलगदादीनि. The works are separate.

samasa.alt: It could be taken as a pañcamī tatpuruṣa with उद्भव in the sense ‘sprung’ (नन्दनात् उद्भवः); but उद्भव is an action noun ‘origin’, so the bahuvrīhi is the natural analysis. The sense is the same.

samasa.sense: fragrant substances and anointing pastes, two of the offerings of worship
samasa.alt: Also possible as a tatpuruṣa, ‘with fragrant unguents’ (गन्धयुक्तानि अनुलेपनानि); with तथा marking a further class of offering, the dvandva reads more naturally.

mantras.anvaya: एवं सुरैः स्तुता, दिव्यैः नन्दनोद्भवैः कुसुमैः तथा गन्धानुलेपनैः अर्चिता जगतां धात्री (4.30 … प्राह)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The sentence runs into 4.30: two participial phrases (स्तुता …, अर्चिता …) describe the subject जगतां धात्री, whose verb is प्राह in the next verse.
mantras.lit: Thus praised by the gods, worshipped with heavenly flowers grown in Nandana, and likewise with perfumes and unguents, the sustainer of the worlds —
mantras.tr: Praised in this way by the gods, and honoured with heavenly flowers from the garden of Nandana, with perfumes and with fragrant pastes, the Mother of the worlds —
mantras.tr_note: धात्री is rendered ‘Mother’, its common sense of nurse and sustainer; the sentence is completed in 4.30.

comm.t: Medhas describes what followed the hymn: the gods do not stop at words but worship the Goddess with flowers from Nandana, Indra’s pleasure-garden, and with perfumes and unguents. The incense follows in 4.30.

Flowers, fragrance and (in the next verse) incense are among the standard upacāras of pūjā. In the story the gods perform for the Goddess the worship that her devotees go on to offer when the text is recited.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name जगद्धात्री (935), ‘sustainer of the world’; the Devī Māhātmya says the same in two words, जगतां धात्री. The two texts remain separate works.

samasa.vigraha: त्रिः आवृत्ताः दश परिमाणम् एषाम्, तैः
samasa.literal: those whose count is three tens
samasa.sense: the gods, the ‘Thirty’, a round figure for the thirty-three gods of the Veda
samasa.alt: A traditional etymology reads तृतीया दशा (यौवनम्) येषां ते, ‘those who are ever in the third stage of life (youth)’, i.e. the ageless gods; also a bahuvrīhi. The numerical reading is the usual one.

samasa.vigraha: प्रसादेन सुमुखी (सुमुखी = शोभनं मुखं यस्याः सा)
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa, its second member a bahuvrīhi
samasa.sense: her face showing her pleasure and grace
samasa.alt: Also read as a pañcamī (cause) relation, प्रसादात् सुमुखी, ‘fair-faced because pleased’; the sense is the same.

morph.note: आह is the substitute that √ब्रू takes in the present (laṭ) parasmaipada, first five endings (आह, आहतुः, आहुः, आत्थ, आहथुः). It is used in narrative for ‘said’. Some grammarians instead treat आह as a perfect of a defective root अह्; either way it means ‘said’.
Denominative-causative stem धूपय- ‘to perfume with incense’ + kta with iṭ: धूपित, ‘censed’. The cognate noun धूपैः stands beside it (‘censed with incense’).
प्र + √नम् + kta: the nasal is lost before -ta (नत), and n becomes ṇ after प्र: प्रणत, ‘bowed’.

mantras.anvaya: (एवं स्तुता अर्चिता जगतां धात्री) समस्तैः त्रिदशैः भक्त्या दिव्यैः धूपैः तु धूपिता प्रसादसुमुखी (सती) समस्तान् प्रणतान् सुरान् प्राह।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main verb प्राह completes the sentence begun in 4.29; its subject is जगतां धात्री, described by a third participle (धूपिता) and the adjective प्रसादसुमुखी. सुरान् is the person addressed.
mantras.lit: and censed with devotion by all the Thirty with heavenly incenses, she, fair-faced with favour, spoke to all the gods, who were bowed down.
mantras.tr: and when all the gods had devoutly offered her heavenly incense, she, her face bright with grace, spoke to the whole company of gods as they bowed before her.

comm.t: The sentence that began in 4.29 ends here. Praise, flowers, unguents and incense are followed by the Goddess’s favour, which shows on her face (प्रसादसुमुखी). The fierce face that terrified Mahiṣa (4.13) is now a gracious one.
Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess सुमुखी (459) and सद्यःप्रसादिनी (383, ‘quickly gracious’). The Devī Māhātmya joins the two ideas in one epithet, प्रसादसुमुखी.

mantras.anvaya_en: A passive imperative with a relative clause as its subject: ‘let (that) be chosen which is desired from us’; the correlative तत् is understood.
mantras.lit: Let it be chosen, O all you Thirty, whatever is desired from us.
mantras.tr: All you gods, choose whatever you desire of me.
mantras.tr_note: The passive imperative is rendered as an active ‘choose’, and the plural of majesty (अस्मत्तः) as ‘me’.

comm.t: A half-verse: the Goddess, pleased by the hymn and the worship, offers the gods a boon. This is the classical response of a deity to praise, and it sets up the request that follows (4.34–37).

The same pattern returns at the end of the Uttama Carita: after the hymn to Nārāyaṇī the Goddess says वरदाहं सुरगणा वरं यन्मनसेच्छथ (11.37), and the gods again ask for the destruction of their enemies and the removal of every affliction.

mantras.tr: You, Blessed One, have done everything; nothing is left to be done.
mantras.tr_note: The respectful third person भगवत्या is turned into the second person ‘you’.

comm.t: A half-verse. The gods’ first answer is that they need nothing more: what they asked for has been accomplished. The reason is given in the next line (4.35): Mahiṣa is dead.
A modern reading: the gods begin by declaring themselves content before they ask anything, and when they do ask, it is for protection and for others (4.36–37).

samasa.sense: Supreme Ruler — the feminine of Śiva’s title Maheśvara
samasa.alt: महत् takes the form महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya, then महा + ईश्वरी → महेश्वरी.

morph.note: नि + √हन् + kta: the root’s nasal is lost before -ta (हत): ‘struck down, slain’.
Gerundive of √दा with the kṛtya affix yat; the ā becomes e before it: देय, ‘to be given’. With the agent in the instrumental (त्वया) it forms an impersonal ‘must/should be given by you’.
The genitive plural appears twice: first possessive (‘our enemy’), then for the recipient (‘to us’), where classical prose would often use the dative.

mantras.anvaya: यत् अयम् अस्माकं शत्रुः महिषासुरः निहतः, (अतः सर्वं कृतम्)। (हे) महेश्वरि, यदि च अपि त्वया अस्माकं वरः देयः, (4.36 …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a causal clause (यत् … निहतः) explaining 4.34. The second line is a conditional (यदि …) whose main clause comes in 4.36: ‘if a boon is still to be given, (then) …’.
mantras.lit: in that this Mahiṣāsura, our enemy, has been slain. And if even so a boon is to be given to us by you, O Great Sovereign, —
mantras.tr: for Mahiṣāsura, our enemy, lies slain. Yet if you would still grant us a boon, O Supreme Sovereign, —
mantras.tr_note: The gerundive ‘is to be given by you’ is rendered ‘if you would grant’; the sentence continues in 4.36.

comm.t: The first line gives the reason for 4.34: the enemy who drove the gods from heaven (2.1–8) is dead. The second line turns, politely and conditionally, to the request; the boon itself is named in 4.36–37.
महेश्वरी, the feminine of Maheśvara, Śiva’s title, names the Goddess as sovereign in her own right. The gods’ courtesy — ‘if a boon is still to be given’ — is the tone in which the text has them ask.

morph.note: Repetition of a word (āmreḍita) expresses ‘again and again, every time’: संस्मृता संस्मृता, ‘remembered each time’. The participle has a conditional force: ‘(when) remembered’.

Optative in -ethāḥ (stem in -a + -īthāḥ), the ātmanepada ending, from a root classically conjugated in the seventh class and parasmaipada (optative हिंस्याः). Such forms are common in epic and Purāṇic Sanskrit (ārṣa). Compare भवेथाः in 4.37.
Simple future of √स्तु: guṇa of u (स्तो-) + -sya-, with s becoming ṣ after o: स्तोष्यति. √स्तु is aniṭ, so no connecting -i-.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अमलानने, संस्मृता संस्मृता त्वं नः परमापदः हिंसेथाः। यः च मर्त्यः एभिः स्तवैः त्वां स्तोष्यति, (4.37 तस्य …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is the main clause of the conditional begun in 4.35 (‘if a boon is to be given, may you destroy …’). The second line opens a relative clause (यः …) whose correlative तस्य comes in 4.37.
mantras.lit: Remembered, remembered, may you destroy our gravest calamities; and whatever mortal will praise you with these hymns, O you of stainless face, —
mantras.tr: whenever we call you to mind, destroy our worst calamities. And whoever among mortals praises you with these hymns, O Goddess of the stainless face, —
mantras.tr_note: The repeated participle is rendered ‘whenever we call you to mind’; the sentence of the second line continues in 4.37.

comm.t: The gods ask two boons. The first is for themselves: that the Goddess, whenever remembered, should destroy their gravest calamities. The second, begun here and completed in 4.37, is for any human being who praises her with ‘these hymns’, the hymn of 4.2–27.

With these two verses the hymn acquires its fruit (phala) for later reciters. The Goddess herself confirms the promise at length in chapter 12, the Phalastuti, which opens in almost the same words: एभिः स्तवैश्च मां नित्यं स्तोष्यते यः समाहितः (12.2).
A modern reading: the gods, once rescued, ask for help not only for themselves but for every person who will ever say their words. Gratitude turns into intercession.

samasa.sense: favourable to the gods who ask
samasa.alt: अस्मत् could also be read as a separate ablative plural, ‘pleased (by our praise) from us’; the printed text joins it, and ‘gracious to us’ is the natural sense.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) अम्बिके, अस्मत्प्रसन्ना त्वं सर्वदा तस्य वित्तर्द्धिविभवैः धनदारादिसम्पदां वृद्धये भवेथाः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause of the relative sentence begun in 4.36 (यः … स्तोष्यति — तस्य …). The genitive तस्य goes with धनदारादिसम्पदाम्; the instrumental वित्तर्द्धिविभवैः is loosely attached, best taken as ‘in respect of wealth …’ with वृद्धये.
mantras.lit: for the increase of his possessions — riches, wife and the rest — in wealth, prosperity and splendour, may you, gracious to us, always be (present), O Ambikā.
mantras.tr: may you, O Mother, ever gracious to us, be with that person always, to increase his wealth, prosperity and fortune, his riches, his wife and family, and all he has.
mantras.tr_note: The loose instrumental and the genitive are rendered together as a list of what increases; ‘be with that person’ makes explicit the sense of भवेथाः … वृद्धये, ‘be (there) for the increase’.

comm.t: The second boon, completed: whoever recites ‘these hymns’ should be granted increase in every worldly good — wealth, prosperity, splendour, riches, wife and household. The gods ask the Goddess to be always gracious to them, and so to him.

The two boons together — protection from calamity when remembered (4.36) and prosperity for the reciter (4.37) — are the fruits the tradition attaches to the Śakrādi stuti. They are the first statement in the text of the reward of recitation, set out in full by the Goddess in chapter 12.
A modern reading: the text does not separate devotion from ordinary life. Wealth, home and family are asked for openly, as things the Goddess is glad to increase.

flags.uncertain: The construction of the instrumental वित्तर्द्धिविभवैः is loose: it may go with वृद्धये (‘increase in wealth …’) or be read as a list parallel to धनदारादिसम्पदाम्. The meaning is the same either way; the reading of the text is not in doubt.

mantras.anvaya_en: The subject भद्रकाली is described by the participle प्रसादिता; the absolutive उक्त्वा precedes the main verb बभूव with its predicate अन्तर्हिता.
mantras.lit: Thus propitiated by the gods for the sake of the world and likewise of themselves, Bhadrakālī said ‘So be it’ and became vanished, O king.
mantras.tr: So the gods entreated her, for the world’s sake and for their own; and Bhadrakālī said, ‘So be it,’ and vanished from their sight, O king.

comm.t: The Goddess grants the boons with one word, तथा, ‘so be it’, and disappears. Medhas reminds his listener (नृप, King Suratha) that he is telling a story. The gods asked both for the world (जगतः) and for themselves (आत्मनः), and both requests were granted.

Here the narrative names her Bhadrakālī, the auspicious Kālī. The liturgical tradition of the Gita Press pāṭha assigns the Madhyama Carita to Mahālakṣmī; the Purāṇa itself moves freely between names for the one Goddess. Her vanishing completes this manifestation; she appears again when needed, as she promises in 11.54–55.

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (with the affix ṇini), containing ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas

samasa.sense: who wishes well to all three worlds

morph.note: Passive participle of the curādi root √कथ्: the stem’s -ay- is dropped and iṭ inserted, कथित. With इति एतत् it makes a closing formula: ‘thus this has been told’.
Past participle of an intransitive verb, so active in meaning: ‘(she) arose’, not ‘was produced’.
The last member -एषिन् is √इष् ‘to seek, wish’ + ṇini (a habitual agent: ‘one who regularly seeks’), feminine in -ī: हितैषिणी, ‘well-wisher’.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) भूप, जगत्त्रयहितैषिणी सा देवी पुरा देवशरीरेभ्यः यथा सम्भूता, (तत्) एतत् इति कथितम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: A main clause (इति एतत् कथितम्) followed by an indirect question of manner (यथा … सम्भूता) that says what ‘this’ was.
mantras.lit: Thus this has been told, O king: how she, the Devī, wishing the welfare of the three worlds, formerly arose from the bodies of the gods.
mantras.tr: So, O king, I have told you how long ago the Goddess, who seeks the good of the three worlds, came forth from the bodies of the gods.
mantras.tr_note: The impersonal passive ‘this has been told’ is rendered ‘I have told you’.

comm.t: Medhas sums up the Madhyama Carita (chapters 2–4) by its first event: the Goddess arose from the gathered splendour of the gods’ bodies (2.9–13) to destroy Mahiṣa. The epithet जगत्त्रयहितैषिणी names her purpose.

In the first carita the Goddess appears from Viṣṇu’s body as Yoganidrā; in the second, from the bodies of all the gods; in the third (announced in the next verse), from Gaurī’s body. The tradition reads these three emergences as one Goddess taking form in different ways.

morph.note: Imperfect of √भू with augment a- and guṇa (भव-): ‘came to be’. With the participle समुद्भूता: ‘how, having arisen, she came to be’.
A dvandva of two names takes the dual: genitive dual in -योः.
Two prefixes, सम् + उत्, on √भू: ‘to arise fully, spring up’; the past participle of this intransitive verb is active in sense.

mantras.anvaya: पुनः च सा गौरीदेहात् समुद्भूता दुष्टदैत्यानां तथा शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः वधाय यथा अभवत्, (4.42 …)
mantras.anvaya_en: A second indirect question of manner (यथा … अभवत्), continued in 4.42 and taken up there by तत्.
mantras.lit: And again how she, having arisen from Gaurī’s body, came to be, for the slaying of the wicked Daityas and likewise of Śumbha and Niśumbha,
mantras.tr: and how once more she arose, this time from the body of Gaurī, to slay the wicked Daityas, and Śumbha and Niśumbha with them,
mantras.tr_note: ‘This time’ makes explicit the contrast with 4.40 that पुनः implies; the sentence continues in 4.42.

comm.t: Medhas announces the third story, the Uttama Carita (chapters 5–13): the Goddess will arise again, from the body of Gaurī, to destroy Śumbha, Niśumbha and their Daityas. In chapter 5 Ambikā comes forth from Pārvatī’s bodily sheath and is called Kauśikī (5.85–87).
The liturgical tradition of the Gita Press pāṭha assigns the Uttama Carita to Mahāsarasvatī, as it assigns the first to Mahākālī and the second to Mahālakṣmī.

morph.note: Imperative of √श्रु (stem शृणु-, with the class-5 nu) with the ātmanepada ending -sva (ṣ after u): शृणुष्व. Classical Sanskrit has only the parasmaipada शृणु; the ātmanepada form is common in epic and Purāṇic verse.
Present of the curādi stem कथय-. A present used of what the speaker is about to do stands for the near future: ‘I am going to tell’.
उप + √कृ + ṇini (habitual agent), feminine उपकारिणी: ‘one who habitually helps’.
आ + √ख्या + kta: आख्यात, ‘told’. With मया: ‘(that) told by me’, i.e. as I tell it.

mantras.anvaya: (सा) च लोकानां रक्षणाय देवानाम् उपकारिणी (यथा अभवत्), तत् मया आख्यातं शृणुष्व; (अहं) ते यथावत् कथयामि।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line ends the indirect question begun in 4.41 (‘how she came to be … for the protection of the worlds, the helper of the gods’). तत् takes up the whole of it as the object of शृणुष्व; a short main clause follows (यथावत् कथयामि ते).
mantras.lit: and for the protection of the worlds, the helper of the gods — hear that, told by me; I tell it to you as it was.
mantras.tr: and to protect the worlds, ever the helper of the gods. Listen as I tell it; I shall tell it to you just as it happened.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Ever’ renders the habitual sense of the ṇini affix in उपकारिणी; the future ‘shall tell’ renders the present कथयामि of imminent action.

comm.t: The last mantra of chapter 4 and of the Madhyama Carita. Medhas finishes announcing the third story — the Goddess’s rising from Gaurī for the slaying of Śumbha and Niśumbha and for the protection of the worlds — and promises to tell it exactly. Chapter 5 begins it.
In the Gita Press pāṭha the chapter closes with the recitation bījas ह्रीं ॐ, printed after the verse. They belong to the pāṭha, not to the Purāṇa, and are not part of the verse’s words.
